summary.text: If $F_{33}$ is prime, its totient is $2^{2^{33}}$, and any smaller positive integer has totient too small to be divisible by that power of two. If $F_{33}$ is composite, a smaller witness than $2^{2^{33}+1}$ would have totient exactly $2^{2^{33}}$: an even witness contradicts $2\phi(m)\le m$, while for an odd witness every prime divisor must be a distinct Fermat prime $F_j$ with $j<33$, whose contributions to the $2$-adic valuation sum to at most $\sum_{j<33}2^j=2^{33}-1$, rather than the required $2^{33}$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^n\mid \varphi(m)\},
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. Put
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1=2^N+1.
\]
We prove that
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]

We will use several elementary facts about the totient function and Fermat primes.

First, for every \(t\ge 0\),
\[
\varphi(2^{t+1})=2^t.
\]
Thus \(2^{N+1}\) always belongs to the set defining \(a(N)\), since
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N.
\]
In particular, that set is nonempty.

Second, if \(q\) is prime, then \(\varphi(q)=q-1\). Hence, if \(F_i=2^{2^i}+1\) is prime, then
\[
\varphi(F_i)=F_i-1=2^{2^i}.
\]
Consequently, when \(F_{33}\) is prime, it also belongs to the set defining \(a(N)\).

Third, if \(m>1\), then
\[
\varphi(m)<m.
\]
Indeed, among the integers from \(1\) to \(m\), the integer \(m\) itself is not relatively prime to \(m\).

We also need the following inequality for even integers:
\[
2\varphi(m)\le m\qquad\text{whenever }m\text{ is even}.
\]
To see this, write \(m=2^e u\), where \(e\ge 1\) and \(u\) is odd. Since \(2^e\) and \(u\) are coprime,
\[
\varphi(m)=\varphi(2^e)\varphi(u)=2^{e-1}\varphi(u).
\]
As \(\varphi(u)\le u\), it follows that
\[
2\varphi(m)=2^e\varphi(u)\le 2^e u=m.
\]

The main auxiliary result is the following.

**Lemma.** If \(m\) is odd and
\[
\varphi(m)=2^{2^{33}}=2^N,
\]
then \(F_{33}\) is prime.

**Proof of the lemma.** Let \(p\) be any prime divisor of \(m\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(p\ne2\). If the exponent of \(p\) in the prime factorization of \(m\) is \(e\ge1\), the prime-power factorization formula for the totient contains the factor
\[
\varphi(p^e)=p^{e-1}(p-1).
\]
In particular,
\[
p-1\mid\varphi(m)=2^N.
\]
Every positive divisor of a power of \(2\) is itself a power of \(2\), so
\[
p-1=2^r
\]
for some \(r\) with \(0\le r\le N\). Because \(p\ne2\), we cannot have \(r=0\): that would give \(p=2\). Thus \(r>0\), and
\[
p=2^r+1
\]
is prime.

We now recall why primality of \(2^r+1\), with \(r>0\), forces \(r\) to be a power of \(2\). Write
\[
r=2^j u
\]
with \(u\) odd. If \(u>1\), set \(x=2^{2^j}\). Since \(u\) is odd,
\[
x^u+1
\]
is divisible by \(x+1\), by the factorization
\[
x^u+1=(x+1)(x^{u-1}-x^{u-2}+\cdots-x+1).
\]
Both factors are then greater than \(1\), so \(x^u+1=2^r+1\) would be composite. Therefore \(u=1\), and hence
\[
r=2^j.
\]
It follows that every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) has the form
\[
p=2^{2^j}+1=F_j
\]
for some \(j\). Moreover, because \(2^j=r\le N=2^{33}\), we have
\[
j\le33.
\]

For each distinct prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\), choose the corresponding index \(j(p)\), so that
\[
p=F_{j(p)}.
\]
These indices are distinct for distinct prime divisors: if \(j(p)=j(q)\), then
\[
p=F_{j(p)}=F_{j(q)}=q.
\]

Let \(v_2(x)\) denote the exponent of \(2\) in a positive integer \(x\). From the prime factorization
\[
m=\prod_{p\mid m}p^{e_p}
\]
and the totient formula, we have
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}p^{e_p-1}(p-1),
\]
where the product is over the distinct prime divisors of \(m\). Every such \(p\) is odd, so the factor \(p^{e_p-1}\) contributes no factor of \(2\). On the other hand,
\[
p-1=F_{j(p)}-1=2^{2^{j(p)}},
\]
so
\[
v_2(p-1)=2^{j(p)}.
\]
Taking \(2\)-adic valuations in the product formula gives
\[
v_2(\varphi(m))=\sum_{p\mid m}2^{j(p)}.
\]
Since \(\varphi(m)=2^N\), its \(2\)-adic valuation is \(N\). Therefore
\[
\sum_{p\mid m}2^{j(p)}=N=2^{33}. \tag{1}
\]

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(F_{33}\) is not prime. Then no prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) can have \(j(p)=33\), since that would say that the prime \(p\) equals \(F_{33}\). We already know that every \(j(p)\le33\), so in fact every index occurring in the sum (1) lies in
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,32\}.
\]
Because the indices are distinct, the sum is at most the sum of all powers of \(2\) with these indices:
\[
\sum_{p\mid m}2^{j(p)}
\le \sum_{j=0}^{32}2^j
=2^{33}-1.
\]
This contradicts (1), according to which the sum is \(2^{33}\). Hence \(F_{33}\) must be prime. This proves the lemma.

We now handle the two cases in the statement.

### Case 1: \(F_{33}\) is prime

As noted above,
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1=2^N,
\]
so \(F_{33}\) is an admissible value in the definition of \(a(N)\). It remains to prove that no smaller positive integer is admissible.

Suppose that \(m<F_{33}=2^N+1\), with \(m>0\), and suppose that
\[
2^N\mid\varphi(m).
\]
Because \(N>0\), \(m\ne1\): indeed, \(\varphi(1)=1\), which is not divisible by \(2^N>1\). Thus \(m>1\), and so
\[
\varphi(m)<m.
\]
The inequality \(m<2^N+1\), with \(m\) integral, gives \(m\le2^N\). Therefore
\[
\varphi(m)<m\le2^N.
\]
On the other hand, \(\varphi(m)>0\) and \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\), so necessarily
\[
\varphi(m)\ge2^N,
\]
a contradiction. Hence no admissible positive integer is smaller than \(F_{33}\), and consequently
\[
a(N)=F_{33}
\]
when \(F_{33}\) is prime.

### Case 2: \(F_{33}\) is not prime

We always have
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N,
\]
so \(2^{N+1}\) is admissible. We prove that no smaller positive integer is admissible.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(m\) is positive,
\[
m<2^{N+1},
\]
and
\[
2^N\mid\varphi(m).
\]
Again \(m\ne1\), because \(\varphi(1)=1\) is not divisible by \(2^N>1\). Hence \(m>1\), and therefore
\[
\varphi(m)<m<2^{N+1}=2\cdot2^N.
\]
Since \(\varphi(m)\) is a positive multiple of \(2^N\), while being strictly less than \(2\cdot2^N\), the only possibility is
\[
\varphi(m)=2^N. \tag{2}
\]

We split according to the parity of \(m\).

If \(m\) is even, the inequality proved earlier gives
\[
2\varphi(m)\le m.
\]
Using (2), this becomes
\[
2^{N+1}\le m,
\]
contrary to \(m<2^{N+1}\).

If \(m\) is odd, equation (2) and the lemma imply that \(F_{33}\) is prime. This contradicts the assumption of the present case that \(F_{33}\) is not prime.

Thus neither parity is possible, and no admissible \(m\) lies below \(2^{N+1}\). Since \(2^{N+1}\) itself is admissible, we conclude that
\[
a(N)=2^{N+1}
\]
when \(F_{33}\) is not prime.

Finally, recalling that \(N=2^{33}=8589934592\), we have established
\[
a(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
2^{2^{33}}+1=F_{33},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
This is exactly the claimed conditional value of the sequence term.
